ADIV: Dividend paying companies across the Asia Pacific region, led by banks with technology and consumer firms behind, all picked for sustainable payouts. It targets income from Asia's growing economies, so it mixes yield with exposure to currencies and markets that swing more than US stocks.
AGQI: Dividend paying companies around the world, chosen for quality and income across technology, banks, industrials and everyday consumer brands. It aims for a global income stream from stocks rather than bonds, so it still moves like a stock fund, just with a steadier, payer focused tilt.
ARLU: Options on the S&P 500 set each April for a one year outcome period, cushioning the first 15 percent of losses while leaving gains uncapped after a small starting hurdle. It swaps the usual cap for a slow start on gains, a different shape of downside protection.
BAMB: US Treasury bonds and high quality corporate bonds maturing within about ten years, managed actively for interest income. It is a middle of the road bond holding: steadier than long term bonds, with a bit more yield and movement than short term ones.
BBSB: US Treasury bonds maturing in one to three years, the short end of government debt. It pays modest interest with very small price swings, serving as a low risk parking place that still earns more than cash, and it barely reacts when interest rates move.
BCEM: Growth companies in emerging markets, hand picked with a long term owner's mindset, led by Asian technology with banks and industrials behind. The managers hold relatively few names for years at a time, so it behaves like a concentrated bet on developing world businesses.
BGLD: Options on a gold fund in a quarterly buffer design: gains on gold are capped each quarter in exchange for a cushion against drops over the same stretch. It suits gold holders who want a smoother ride, trading away part of a big gold rally for downside softness.
BTGD: Full exposure to bitcoin and full exposure to gold at the same time, stacked through futures so each dollar carries both bets at once. The pairing mixes a wild digital asset with a classic haven, and the built in leverage means both can hit the fund together.
CANE: Sugar futures contracts, rolled as they expire, giving direct exposure to the world sugar price without owning any physical sugar. It is a single commodity trading tool that swings with harvests, weather and energy markets, and futures rolling costs can eat into returns over time.
CDIG: Stocks from around the world picked freely by the managers across industries and company sizes, currently leaning toward consumer, energy and utility companies. With no index to follow, results depend on the managers' calls, making it a go anywhere equity holding.
COAL: Coal companies worldwide, miners and shippers of both power plant coal and the metallurgical coal used to make steel. It is a narrow, old economy bet that rises and falls with coal prices and energy demand, and few other funds still offer this exposure.
DEEF: Large companies in developed countries outside the US, screened by several factors at once, including value, quality and momentum, with industrials the biggest slice. The multifactor screen aims to beat a plain foreign index over time, though it can trail for stretches when its factors fall out of favor.
EVYM: High yield municipal bonds, the riskier end of tax exempt debt, issued by cities, hospitals, housing projects and other public borrowers with weaker credit. The interest is generally free from federal income tax and pays more than safer munis, in exchange for more default risk.
FFGX: Growth companies outside the US, picked by bottom up fundamental research across developed and emerging markets, with technology and banks the largest slices. It is an actively managed foreign growth holding, so its fate rests on stock picking rather than any single country's market.
FLMB: Long term municipal bonds chosen to fund environmental projects, whose interest is free from federal income tax. The green label is the twist on a classic tax exempt income fund, and the long maturities mean its price moves more when interest rates change.
HRTS: Health care companies working on heart disease and weight related treatments, especially the GLP-1 drug wave and cardiovascular therapies. It is a focused bet on two huge treatment markets, so trial results and drug approvals can move it sharply.
IFEB: Options on a developed markets stock fund covering Europe, Japan and other rich countries outside the US, set each February for a one year outcome period with a loss cushion and capped gains. It brings defined outcome protection to foreign stocks, adding currency swings on top.
IWMW: Small US companies held through a small cap stock fund, plus call options sold on that small cap basket each month to generate income. Selling the calls trades away part of small caps' upside, so it aims for steadier payouts from a jumpy corner of the market.
KWH: Companies that build and run power infrastructure: utilities, grid equipment makers, engineering firms and energy suppliers, positioned for rising electricity demand worldwide. It is a focused bet on electrification, from data centers to electric vehicles, so it moves with energy and industrial cycles.
MARO: An options income strategy tied to MARA, a bitcoin mining company, using contracts that give indirect exposure to its share price while collecting option premiums for payouts. It rises and falls with one volatile crypto linked stock, and its gains are capped, so the income is the point.
MEM: Emerging market stocks picked actively for sustainable growth, heavy in Asian technology with banks and consumer companies behind. It roams the developing world including China, so it offers broader emerging exposure with stock picking on top, and swings with those volatile markets.
MNBD: Intermediate term municipal bonds issued by US states, cities and public projects, whose interest is generally free from federal income tax. It is built for steady tax exempt income with modest swings, suiting taxable accounts more than retirement accounts where the tax break is wasted.
MSSE: A trust that holds ether, the cryptocurrency of the Ethereum network, and stakes part of it, locking it up to help run the network in exchange for extra rewards. It gives stock market access to ether's price, which swings far more than most investments.
NCPB: A core bond portfolio with extra reach: investment grade bonds form the base, and managers can add higher yielding debt for more income. It aims to beat plain core bond funds over time by flexing across sectors, accepting somewhat more credit risk.
NIKL: Nickel mining companies, the explorers and producers of the metal used in stainless steel and electric vehicle batteries. It is a narrow commodity stock bet, so it swings with nickel prices and battery demand rather than the broad mining market.
NTSE: Emerging market stocks, heavy in Asian technology, layered with US Treasury futures on top so each dollar works twice. The stacked design aims for stock growth plus bond returns from the same money, and the leverage can magnify losses as well as gains.
NUDV: US companies that pay high dividends and also pass environmental, social and governance screens, led by banks, health care and industrials. It pairs income with values screening, so heavy polluters and poor governance scorers are left out even when their dividends are tempting.
NXTE: Companies worldwide picked for sustainability, from clean technology and health care to industrials and real estate, with technology about half the fund. It is a values driven growth holding: the screen favors firms judged greener than their peers, which tilts it toward tech and away from heavy polluters.
OCTT: Options on the S&P 500 set each October for a one year outcome period, absorbing the first 10 percent of losses while capping gains. It suits investors who want large US stock exposure with a planned cushion, and the terms reset every October.
PFI: Financial companies only: banks, insurers, asset managers and real estate firms, narrowed to a few dozen names showing the strongest recent price momentum. Concentrating on one sector and chasing its hottest stocks makes it a focused, jumpier bet than a plain financial fund.
PMIO: Municipal bonds from across the US, actively hunted for income opportunities in issues other buyers overlook, with interest generally free from federal income tax. It aims to pay more than plain muni index funds by taking selective credit risks within the tax exempt market.
PSR: US real estate investment trusts and property companies, picked actively rather than by index, spanning apartments, warehouses, offices, malls and other property types. It pays income from rents collected across the property market, and it rises and falls with real estate values and interest rates.
QBQV: Options on the Nasdaq-100 growth basket set for one year outcome periods, absorbing the first 5 percent of losses in exchange for capped gains. The cushion is thinner than most buffer funds offer, which leaves more upside room but less protection when tech stocks slide.
QFF: US growth companies chosen as quality compounders: businesses with durable advantages, high returns on capital and managers who reinvest profits wisely, led by technology, banks and consumer names. The focus on proven operators makes it a steady handed growth holding that depends on a focused list of stocks.
QLDY: Options on the Nasdaq-100 traded through daily call spreads, a strategy designed to harvest small amounts of income every day and pay distributions twice a week. It barely owns the underlying stocks' upside, so it is an income machine built on tech volatility, with daily resets and high turnover.
QQQA: Just twenty one stocks at a time: the members of a big Nasdaq growth index with the strongest recent price momentum, swapped as momentum shifts, with technology usually dominating. Concentrating on the hottest slice of a growth index makes it a turbocharged, swing heavy bet.
REIT: US real estate investment trusts picked actively across property types like apartments, warehouses, shopping centers and offices. Active picking is the difference from index REIT funds: managers can dodge weak property sectors, and the income comes from rents the trusts collect.
RSPC: The communication services companies of the large US stock market, internet platforms, media, entertainment and telecom, held in equal weights rather than by size. Equal weighting gives smaller names a real voice next to the giants, so it behaves differently from the usual giant led sector fund.
SJB: A short term trading tool that moves opposite to high yield corporate bonds each day, gaining when junk bonds fall and losing when they rise. Because the inverse exposure resets daily, it is built for brief hedges or bets, not for holding through long stretches.
SURE: US companies chosen by watching what corporate insiders do: stocks where executives are buying their own shares or the company is buying back stock get the nod. The idea is that insiders know their businesses best, making this a signal driven twist on stock picking.
TBLU: Water companies worldwide: utilities that deliver drinking water, plus makers of pipes, pumps, meters and treatment equipment, with industrials about three fifths of the fund. It is a focused bet on the business of clean water, a steadier theme than most single industry funds.
THLV: A basket of US stock funds held in equal weights and selected by rules meant to keep volatility low, with the mix adjusted as conditions change. It aims for a smoother ride through the stock market, and the large cash stake it can hold will drag when markets climb steadily.
THMZ: Established large companies around the world, including emerging markets, chosen for their place in long running megatrends like technology change and health care demand. It is an actively managed global growth holding, spreading bets across industries so no single trend carries the whole fund.
TLIE: Large US companies picked for income and value by a manager known for patient, concentrated stock picking, spread across technology, banks, industrials and health care. It favors profitable payers bought at reasonable prices, aiming for dividends plus steady growth rather than chasing hot stocks.
TSCZ: Bonds backed by loans and property: home mortgages, commercial mortgages, asset backed securities and loan bundles, in both government backed and private forms. It hunts income in the securitized market with active management, offering a different flavor of bond risk than corporate or Treasury funds.
VAIE: Exposure to synthetic autocallable notes tied to large US stocks, instruments that pay regular income while stocks behave and can be called away early when they rise. The catch sits underneath: if the stocks fall past a set barrier, losses can arrive suddenly and run deep.
VEMY: High yield bonds tied to emerging market countries, issued by governments and companies that pay extra interest to compensate for weaker credit. The yield is the draw, and the risks are real: currency swings, politics and defaults all hit harder here than in rich country bonds.
XIJN: Options on the S&P 500 set each June, combining a buffer against losses with an income feature that pays premiums along the way, over a one year outcome period. It mixes two defined outcome ideas, cushion plus income, and like its cousins it caps how much of a rally you keep.
XLUI: Utility companies, the power, gas and water providers known for steady dividends, paired with an options program that sells calls to add premium income. The result aims for dependable payouts from a usually calm sector, giving up some gains when utilities run.
XXV: Treasury interest plus an option spread strategy, combined to target steady distributions that the fund aims to pay out regularly. Most of the money sits in bonds, so the options do the extra work, and payouts can vary with market conditions rather than being guaranteed.
